You are black-box characterizing a compiled Python program at /workspace/dataset/test15_executable.
Its Python source is:

    import argparse, base58
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument('--a', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--b', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--c', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--d', type=str, required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    enc1 = base58.b58encode(args.a.encode())
    enc2 = base58.b58encode(args.b.encode())
    dec1 = base58.b58decode(args.c)
    dec2 = base58.b58decode(args.d)
    print(enc1); print(enc2); print(dec1); print(dec2)

Goal: a Node.js reimplementation must match stdout byte-for-byte and match exit codes.
RUN THE EXECUTABLE MANY TIMES with the Bash tool to establish ground truth. Do NOT use the
`python` command (unavailable/forbidden). Use `cat -A` or `od -c` / hexdump when whitespace or
non-ASCII bytes matter, and always capture the exit code.
Useful trick: to learn the repr of an arbitrary byte string S, first run with --a S to get its
base58 encoding E, then run with --c E to see how Python reprs those exact bytes.
Be rigorous and adversarial: try to break your own hypotheses. Report ONLY what you verified by running.

Resolve this SINGLE open question by actually running the executable. Run every command you need.

QUESTION: Length/performance boundary, flagged but unmeasured by the reports. I measured it: the per-argument limit is MAX_ARG_STRLEN = 131072 INCLUDING the NUL, so 131071 bytes is the largest reachable value and 131072 fails at exec (bash prints 'Argument list too long', rc=126, the program never runs). At that boundary the reference binary is slow because base58's divmod loops are O(n^2): encode of one 131071-byte --a ~13 s, both --a and --b ~26.4 s, decode of 131071 'z' ~7.4 s each, and all four maxed out = 40.9 s wall, rc=0, stdout exactly 946580 bytes / 4 lines. (All-'1' decode is fast: 131071 '1's -> 139 ms, 524308 bytes, 4 lines.) STILL OPEN: whether a Node BigInt port completes inside the grader's timeout at these sizes, and whether it produces byte-identical output there.

Suggested probes (adapt as needed, add more):
  cd /workspace/dataset && A=$(node -e 'process.stdout.write("a".repeat(131071))'); Z=$(node -e 'process.stdout.write("z".repeat(131071))'); s=$(date +%s%N); ./test15_executable --a "$A" --b "$A" --c "$Z" --d "$Z" >/tmp/big 2>&1; rc=$?; e=$(date +%s%N); echo "rc=$rc ms=$(( (e-s)/1000000 )) bytes=$(wc -c </tmp/big) lines=$(wc -l </tmp/big)"; md5sum /tmp/big
  cd /workspace/dataset && B=$(node -e 'process.stdout.write("a".repeat(131072))'); ./test15_executable --a "$B" --b x --c 1 --d 1; echo "rc=$? (expect 126 Argument list too long)"
  cd /workspace/dataset && O=$(node -e 'process.stdout.write("1".repeat(131071))'); s=$(date +%s%N); ./test15_executable --a x --b x --c "$O" --d 1 >/tmp/o; e=$(date +%s%N); echo "rc=$? ms=$(( (e-s)/1000000 )) bytes=$(wc -c </tmp/o)"
  getconf ARG_MAX

Answer definitively with the implementable rule and the raw evidence. If the question turns out to
be unreachable or irrelevant for a Node reimplementation, say so explicitly.

Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
